evidence.text: The entry reports the received Shuowen pictograph explanation as 子 without arms, alongside a commentary interpretation involving entangled legs. It says the relation to ‘finish’ may be a sound loan, while an entangled→tied→finished path is another proposal. It reports the verb ‘finish/be completed’ developing into a perfective particle, common by Tang, and later into a sentence-final change-of-state particle. These are secondary summaries; the page does not establish an early graph referent or dated intermediate semantic links.

evidence.text: Quotes the received Shuowen definition 尦也。从子無臂。象形 and Duan Yucai’s interpretation of crossing legs and twisted or knotted forms (了戾). The same entry reports later meanings including understanding clearly and finishing. These dictionary interpretations do not independently establish the depicted referent or prove the semantic bridge to ‘finish’.

evidence.source: Bolor B., Mongolian Journal of Foreign Languages and Cultures
evidence.text: The article argues the sentential particle and perfective suffix derive from the lexical verb liao ‘finish’. Its abstract dates an inchoative use to texts from the 10th century (late Tang), particle-like functions by the 13th century (late Song), and reports both particles still pronounced [liau] in an 18th-century source. The abstract summarizes the argument but does not supply primary quotations for inspection here.
evidence.title: On the origin of the Mandarin Chinese sentential particle 了 (le)

gaps: No securely dated earliest inscriptional attestation or paleographic sequence for 了 was established; the inspected character-level form-history evidence is a received Shuowen account and secondary form lists.
The Shuowen ‘child without arms’ analysis and the crossed/entangled-legs readings are competing interpretations. No inspected primary artifact image adjudicates them.

The proposed semantic route entangled/twisted→tied→finished lacks dated intermediate examples in inspected sources. A sound-loan account is also not independently established here with an early source spelling and phonological comparison.

The abstract dates grammaticalization stages to late Tang, late Song, and an 18th-century source, but exact primary quotations were not inspected. The further development of final 了 remains summarized through secondary scholarship.

No suitable alternate direct glyph image URL with verified identity and reuse provenance was obtained. The supplied Commons redraw’s exact image URL returned 404 during acquisition and is excluded; Xiaoxuetang’s character-specific result was unavailable, so no image is proposed.
No bulk local source extract is recommended: reuse permission for a repeatable source extract was not verified and the opened references support concise character-specific citation.
